think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 73-year-old female retired nurse who underwent elective reverse total shoulder arthroplasty after 4 years of intractable shoulder destruction (misdiagnosed as rheumatoid arthritis and treated with methotrexate) presents 15 days post-surgery with acute fever, headache, diplopia, and basilar meningitis. The diagnostic tension lies in differentiating acute postoperative nosocomial bacterial meningitis from the reactivation and hematogenous dissemination of occult skeletal tuberculosis unmasked by arthroplasty surgery.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs upon hospital admission for the acute neurological syndrome, after physical examination, shoulder imaging/ultrasound (confirming an intact surgical site), and emergency lumbar puncture (demonstrating hypoglycorrhachia and lymphocytic pleocytosis) are performed, immediately prior to CSF mycobacterial PCR and pending intraoperative histopathology/cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute postoperative nosocomial bacterial meningitis typically occurs within days of surgery and presents with rapid neurological deterioration and neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis with elevated CSF lactate; in contrast, this patient presented with basilar enhancement and a predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis (90% lymphocytes) with profound hypoglycorrhachia. Viral meningoencephalitis causes lymphocytic pleocytosis but normal CSF glucose levels. The combination of chronic humeral osteolysis with a sclerotic rim, previous immunosuppressive exposure (methotrexate), and lymphocytic hypoglycorrhachic basilar meningitis strongly suggests tuberculous meningoencephalitis arising from an undiagnosed tuberculous monoarthritis.
case_prompt:
A 73-year-old female, a retired nurse, presents to the emergency department with acute onset of high fever (38.5°C), general malaise, frontal headaches, and diplopia, occurring fifteen days after undergoing an elective right reverse total shoulder arthroplasty. Four years prior to surgery, she developed debilitating pain and functional impairment of the right shoulder, which had been attributed to inflammatory glenohumeral osteoarthritis secondary to rheumatoid arthritis and treated unsuccessfully with methotrexate (10 mg weekly) for three years. Preoperative workup had demonstrated an ankylosed shoulder with humeral head joint space narrowing, osteolysis of the greater tuberosity with a sclerotic rim, and rotator cuff atrophy; preoperative joint aspiration had yielded clear synovial fluid with 35 leukocytes/mm³ and sterile bacterial cultures after 15 days of incubation.

On physical examination at readmission, the patient is febrile and appears acutely unwell. Neurologic examination reveals diplopia and meningeal signs without focal limb weakness. The right shoulder surgical incision is intact, clean, and well-healed without erythema, discharge, warmth, or tenderness. Postoperative plain radiographs of the shoulder demonstrate stable prosthetic seating, and bedside shoulder ultrasonography reveals no joint fluid or periarticular collections.

Chest radiography reveals clear lung fields without visible infiltrates or cavitation. Emergency brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrates peri-mesencephalic leptomeningeal enhancement compatible with basilar meningitis. Lumbar puncture yields clear cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with marked abnormalities: profound hypoglycorrhachia at 1.0 mmol/L, hypochloremia at 109 mmol/L, hyperproteinorachia at 1.9 g/L, and a pleocytosis of 175 white blood cells/mm², of which 90% are lymphocytes.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: While acute fever, headache, and diplopia 15 days following arthroplasty raised high suspicion for postoperative bacterial meningitis, blood cultures were negative, and CSF analysis demonstrated a marked lymphocytic pleocytosis (90% lymphocytes) rather than the pronounced neutrophilic predominance characteristic of pyogenic bacterial infections.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Blood cultures were negative, retrospectively, and MRI confirmed a peri-mesencephalic meningitis. A lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid hypoglycorrhachia at 1 mmol/L, hypochloremia at 109, hyperproteinorachia at 1.9 g/L, white blood cells at 175/mm2, of which 90% were lymphocytes.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Aseptic Inflammatory Glenohumeral Osteoarthritis / Rheumatoid Flare
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The chronic 4-year history of shoulder impairment had been presumed secondary to rheumatoid arthritis, but it proved completely refractory to 3 years of methotrexate; atypical osteolysis with a sclerotic rim and subsequent acute meningitis indicated that the underlying joint destruction was an occult indolent infection rather than aseptic inflammatory arthritis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The overall history and symptoms were consistent with a diagnosis of glenohumeral osteoarthritis related to rheumatoid arthritis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Specific PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the cerebrospinal fluid returned positive, and delayed histopathological analysis of intraoperative shoulder specimens revealed epithelioid granulomatous lesions, with deep shoulder tissue and CSF cultures confirming pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Specific PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the cerebrospinal fluid was positive... Histopathological examination of intraoperative samples, available 15 days after prosthesis placement, revealed epithelioid granulomatous lesions. Deep sample cultures showed M. tuberculosis susceptible to all tested antituberculosis drugs.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly according to Stanford MedCaseReasoning CPC format. The case_prompt cleanly isolates Day 1 emergency readmission triage and CSF baseline labs before CSF PCR and intraoperative histology results return. Zero pathogen spoilers in prompt.
